introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c)**

Figure 5 shows a set-up used to determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

The calorimeter has a mass of $200\ \mathrm{g}$ and a specific heat capacity of $385\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

(i) Explain why the liquid is stirred during the experiment and why the calorimeter is insulated.

(ii) After heating for $180\ \mathrm{s}$, the temperature of the liquid increases from $20.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $37.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. If the mass of the liquid in the calorimeter is $280\ \mathrm{g}$, determine the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

(iii) The length of the liquid column in the above thermometer is $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $36.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What will be the length of the liquid column when the temperature rises to $70.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Stirring and insulation.**

- **Stirring:** the heater warms only the liquid next to it. Stirring spreads the heat quickly and evenly through the liquid (and the calorimeter), so that all of it is at the same temperature and the thermometer shows the true temperature of the whole liquid.
- **Insulation:** it reduces the heat lost to the surroundings, so that almost all the electrical energy supplied goes into heating the liquid and the calorimeter. Without it the measured heat gained would be too small for the energy supplied and the calculated specific heat capacity would be too large.

**(ii) Specific heat capacity of the liquid.** The electrical energy supplied is
$$W = VIt = 12.0\times3.20\times180 = 6.91\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}.$$
Rise in temperature: $\Delta\theta = 37.7 - 20.5 = 17.2\ \mathrm{K}$.

Assuming no heat loss, $W = m_c c_c\Delta\theta + m_l c_l\Delta\theta$. Heat gained by the calorimeter:
$$Q_c = 0.200\times385\times17.2 = 1.32\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}.$$
Heat gained by the liquid: $Q_l = 6912 - 1324 = 5.59\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$, so
$$c_l = \frac{Q_l}{m_l\Delta\theta} = \frac{5588}{0.280\times17.2} = 1.16\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}.$$

**(iii) Length of the liquid column.** The length varies linearly with temperature: the $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ interval corresponds to $36.0 - 3.0 = 33.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. At $70.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$:
$$l = 3.0 + \frac{70.5 - 0}{100 - 0}\times33.0 = 3.0 + 23.3 = 26.3\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Differentiate between the following classes of waves giving one example in each class.

(i) Transverse and longitudinal waves.

(ii) Mechanical and electromagnetic waves.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Transverse and longitudinal waves**

| | Transverse wave | Longitudinal wave |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of vibration | The particles (or fields) vibrate **perpendicular** to the direction of travel of the wave. | The particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction of travel of the wave. |
| Pattern | Crests and troughs. | Compressions and rarefactions. |
| Polarisation | Can be polarised. | Cannot be polarised. |
| Example | Light, or a wave on a stretched string. | Sound in air. |

**(ii) Mechanical and electromagnetic waves**

| | Mechanical wave | Electromagnetic wave |
|---|---|---|
| Medium | Needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel; it cannot travel through a vacuum. | Needs no medium: it can travel through a vacuum. |
| Origin | Vibration of the particles of the medium, which carry the energy on. | Oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. |
| Speed | Depends on the medium (about $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for sound in air). | $3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in a vacuum for all of them. |
| Example | Sound, water waves. | Radio waves, light, X-rays. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 6 below shows two light beams A and B of wavelength $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ travelling in air and incident on a composite crystal of thickness $20\ \mu\mathrm{m}$. The refractive index of X is $1.40$ and that of Y is $1.45$.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_2.png)

(i) Determine which beam will first emerge from the crystal.

(ii) If A and B are in phase as they enter the crystal, calculate their phase difference as they leave the crystal.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for the speed of light in air. Beam A crosses the thickness $d = 20\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ of X and beam B crosses the same thickness of Y.

**(i) First beam to emerge.** The speed of light in a medium of refractive index $n$ is $v = c/n$, so the time to cross is $t = d/v = nd/c$:
$$t_A = \frac{1.40\times20\times10^{-6}}{3.00\times10^{8}} = 9.33\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s},\qquad t_B = \frac{1.45\times20\times10^{-6}}{3.00\times10^{8}} = 9.67\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{s}.$$
$t_A < t_B$ (light travels faster in X, which has the lower refractive index): **beam A emerges first**, ahead of B by $3.3\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{s}$.

**(ii) Phase difference.** The optical path difference is
$$\Delta = (n_Y - n_X)\,d = (1.45 - 1.40)\times20\times10^{-6} = 1.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}.$$
In terms of the wavelength in air: $\dfrac{\Delta}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-6}}{450\times10^{-9}} = 2.22$ wavelengths, so
$$\phi = \frac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda} = 2\pi\times2.22 = 14.0\ \mathrm{rad}\ (\approx 800^\circ).$$
(Check: the numbers of wavelengths in the two blocks are $\dfrac{1.40\times20\ \mu\mathrm{m}}{450\ \mathrm{nm}} = 62.2$ and $\dfrac{1.45\times20\ \mu\mathrm{m}}{450\ \mathrm{nm}} = 64.4$: a difference of $2.22$.)

**The phase difference is about $14.0\ \mathrm{rad}$**, i.e. two complete cycles plus $1.40\ \mathrm{rad}$ ($80^\circ$): the beams leave $80^\circ$ out of phase.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR 6 (d), (e) and (f)**

Figure 7 shows a set-up used by an upper sixth student to measure the speed of sound in air. The audio frequency generator is placed some distance away from the wall and the microphone is placed between them.

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_3.png)

(i) Explain why alternate loud and soft sounds are heard when the microphone is moved between the a.f. signal generator and the wall.

(ii) At position A, the sound is loudest. The microphone is then moved away from A until the softest sound is heard at B. If the sound from the generator has a frequency of $610\ \mathrm{Hz}$, determine the speed of sound in air.

(iii) A motorist riding towards the a.f. signal generator observes that the frequency of sound from the generator is $640\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Use your answer in d)(ii) above to estimate the speed of the motorist.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Loud and soft sounds.** The sound from the generator is reflected by the wall. The incident wave and the reflected wave have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions, so they **superpose to form a stationary (standing) wave** between the generator and the wall. Where the two waves arrive in phase the interference is constructive and the sound is loud (an **antinode** of the sound intensity at the microphone); where they arrive in antiphase the interference is destructive and the sound is soft or zero (a **node**). Moving the microphone along the line therefore passes alternately through loud and soft positions, a loud position and the next soft position being a quarter of a wavelength apart.

**(ii) Speed of sound.** A is a loud position and B is the next soft position, so
$$AB = \frac{\lambda}{4} = 13.5\ \mathrm{cm}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\lambda = 54.0\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.540\ \mathrm{m}.$$
$$v = f\lambda = 610\times0.540 = 329\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ (\approx 3.3\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}).$$

**(iii) Speed of the motorist.** The source is at rest and the observer (the motorist) moves towards it with speed $u$, so the observed frequency is (Doppler effect)
$$f' = f\,\frac{v + u}{v}\quad\Rightarrow\quad u = v\left(\frac{f'}{f} - 1\right) = 329\times\left(\frac{640}{610} - 1\right) = 329\times0.0492 = 16.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$
**The speed of the motorist is about $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$** ($\approx 58\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The light from a filter has a wavelength of $560\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(i) What is the energy, in joules, of each photon of the above light?

(ii) Determine the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons that will be emitted if this light falls on a metal surface with a work function of $1.32\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(iii) Figure 8 shows what happens to one of the electrons with the maximum kinetic energy as it approaches a negatively charged particle with a charge of $3.0\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{C}$.

![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_4.png)

Determine the distance of closest approach, $y$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Constants used: $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$.

**(i) Photon energy.**
$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{560\times10^{-9}} = 3.55\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\ (= 2.22\ \mathrm{eV}).$$

**(ii) Maximum kinetic energy** (Einstein's photoelectric equation $hf = \phi + E_{k,\max}$):
$$E_{k,\max} = 2.22 - 1.32 = 0.90\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.90\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 1.44\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

**(iii) Distance of closest approach.** The electron (charge $-e$) is repelled by the negative particle (charge $Q$). At the closest approach it is momentarily at rest, so all its kinetic energy has been converted to electric potential energy:
$$E_{k,\max} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{Qe}{y}\quad\Rightarrow\quad y = \frac{8.99\times10^{9}\times3.0\times10^{-16}\times1.60\times10^{-19}}{1.44\times10^{-19}} = 3.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}.$$
**The distance of closest approach is $y \approx 3.0\ \mu\mathrm{m}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 9(a) shows a simple a.c. circuit containing a resistor and an inductor while figure 9(b) shows how the a.c. voltage in the circuit varies with time.

![fig-5](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_5.png)

X in the circuit is an appliance that gets destroyed when the peak current through it is above $4.2\ \mathrm{A}$.

(i) Write down the peak voltage and the frequency of the above a.c.

(ii) Show that the total impedance in the circuit is $5.0\ \Omega$.

(iii) Determine, by calculation, whether X will be destroyed.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Peak voltage and frequency.** From figure 9(b) the peak voltage is $V_0 = 12\ \mathrm{V}$. One complete cycle of the sinusoid takes $T = 20\ \mathrm{ms}$ (the mark $20$ is at the end of the first cycle), so
$$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{20\times10^{-3}} = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$

**(ii) Total impedance.** The reactance of the inductor is
$$X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi\times50\times12.7\times10^{-3} = 3.99\ \Omega.$$
The resistor and inductor are in series, with the voltages across them $90^\circ$ out of phase, so
$$Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}} = \sqrt{3.0^{2} + 3.99^{2}} = \sqrt{24.9} = 4.99\ \Omega\approx5.0\ \Omega.\qquad\blacksquare$$

**(iii) Will X be destroyed?** The peak current is
$$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{Z} = \frac{12}{5.0} = 2.4\ \mathrm{A}.$$
Since $2.4\ \mathrm{A} < 4.2\ \mathrm{A}$, **X will not be destroyed.**
